claim: BCL6 is enriched in the fed state in liver
source: Here, we find that the B cell lymphoma 6 (BCL6) repressor is enriched in the fed state and converges genome-wide with PPARα to potently suppress the induction of fasting transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing BCL6 binding patterns and protein expression data in fed vs fasted states

claim: BCL6 converges genome-wide with PPARα
source: Here, we find that the B cell lymphoma 6 (BCL6) repressor is enriched in the fed state and converges genome-wide with PPARα to potently suppress the induction of fasting transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing overlapping binding sites between BCL6 and PPARα

claim: BCL6 potently suppresses the induction of fasting transcription
source: Here, we find that the B cell lymphoma 6 (BCL6) repressor is enriched in the fed state and converges genome-wide with PPARα to potently suppress the induction of fasting transcription.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing gene expression changes in Bcl6 knockout mice

claim: Deletion of hepatocyte Bcl6 enhances lipid catabolism
source: Deletion of hepatocyte Bcl6 enhances lipid catabolism and ameliorates high-fat-diet-induced steatosis.

claim: Deletion of hepatocyte Bcl6 ameliorates high-fat-diet-induced steatosis
source: Deletion of hepatocyte Bcl6 enhances lipid catabolism and ameliorates high-fat-diet-induced steatosis.

claim: Hepatocyte Bcl6 ablation restores enhancer activity at PPARα-dependent genes in Ppara-null mice
source: In Ppara-null mice, hepatocyte Bcl6 ablation restores enhancer activity at PPARα-dependent genes and overcomes defective fasting-induced fatty acid oxidation and lipid accumulation.
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice

claim: Hepatocyte Bcl6 ablation overcomes defective fasting-induced fatty acid oxidation in Ppara-null mice
source: In Ppara-null mice, hepatocyte Bcl6 ablation restores enhancer activity at PPARα-dependent genes and overcomes defective fasting-induced fatty acid oxidation and lipid accumulation.

claim: Hepatocyte Bcl6 ablation overcomes lipid accumulation in Ppara-null mice

claim: BCL6 is a negative regulator of oxidative metabolism
source: Together, these findings identify BCL6 as a negative regulator of oxidative metabolism and reveal that alternating recruitment of repressive and activating transcription factors to shared cis-regulatory regions dictates hepatic lipid handling.

claim: Alternating recruitment of repressive and activating transcription factors to shared cis-regulatory regions dictates hepatic lipid handling

claim: The bacterial lac operon established a central paradigm for transcriptional repression to direct metabolic responses

claim: In the fed state, SREBP and ChREBP direct lipogenesis and glycolysis

source: For each corepressor, binding at BCL6 sites was significantly reduced in Bcl6LKO livers.

claim: Loss of SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 complexes was inversely correlated to H3K27ac at BCL6 sites
source: Moreover, loss of these complexes was inversely correlated to histone 3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac), a marker for enhancer activity (Creyghton et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008), which was significantly elevated along BCL6-SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 sites in Bcl6LKO livers.
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data in Bcl6LKO mice and citations to Creyghton et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008

claim: H3K27ac was significantly elevated along BCL6-SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 sites in Bcl6LKO livers
source: Moreover, loss of these complexes was inversely correlated to histone 3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac), a marker for enhancer activity (Creyghton et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008), which was significantly elevated along BCL6-SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 sites in Bcl6LKO livers.
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data in Bcl6LKO mice

claim: BCL6 recruits a subset of liver SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 complexes
source: Together, these findings revealed a role for BCL6 to recruit a subset of liver SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 complexes and repress associated regulatory regions.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing co-localization and dependence of corepressor binding on BCL6

claim: Differentially expressed transcripts in Bcl6LKO livers are enriched for lipid metabolism, oxidation, and PPAR signaling
source: Gene ontology analysis of differentially expressed transcripts in the livers of Bcl6LKO animals revealed lipid metabolism, oxidation, and PPAR signaling as top scoring terms (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: Fasting upregulated 162 genes and downregulated 174 genes by at least 2-fold in liver
source: Livers from mice restricted from food overnight exhibited 162 genes upregulated and 174 genes downregulated by at least 2-fold using RNA-seq (Figure 4B), and fasting regulated a common set of gene expression pathways with Bcl6 ablation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Over 40% of robustly regulated fasting genes (135/336) were controlled by BCL6
source: Notably, over 40% of robustly regulated fasting genes (135/336) were controlled by BCL6 (Figure 4C, top panel) and for the vast majority, Bcl6 ablation mimicked the impact of fasting on transcription (Figure 4C, bottom panel and Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: For the vast majority of BCL6-controlled fasting genes, Bcl6 ablation mimicked the impact of fasting on transcription
source: Notably, over 40% of robustly regulated fasting genes (135/336) were controlled by BCL6 (Figure 4C, top panel) and for the vast majority, Bcl6 ablation mimicked the impact of fasting on transcription (Figure 4C, bottom panel and Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4D

claim: Gene expression patterns in Bcl6LKO mice more closely resembled profiles from fasting than fed control mice
source: Unsupervised clustering analyses of liver gene expression revealed that patterns in Bcl6LKO mice, irrespective of nutrition status, more closely resembled profiles from fasting than fed control mice (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Genes co-regulated by fasting and Bcl6 deletion are enriched in ontologies for lipid and ketone body metabolism as well as PPARα signaling
source: Genes co-regulated by fasting and Bcl6 deletion are enriched in ontologies for lipid and ketone body metabolism as well as PPARα signaling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Over 50% of fasting-regulated genes contained co-occurring BCL6-PPARα-binding sites
source: Over 50% of these fasting genes contained co-occurring BCL6-PPARα-binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), with a median of two co-occurring sites per gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Fasting-regulated genes with BCL6-PPARα-binding sites have a median of two co-occurring sites per gene
source: Over 50% of these fasting genes contained co-occurring BCL6-PPARα-binding sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), with a median of two co-occurring sites per gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B

claim: Just 24% or 1.4% of fasting genes contained PPARα-only or BCL6-only sites, respectively
source: By contrast, just 24% or 1.4% of fasting genes contained PPARα-only or BCL6-only sites, respectively, and these occurred with a median of just one regulatory region per gene.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Fasting-regulated genes with BCL6-PPARα regulatory elements exhibited significantly greater ranges of expression than those with PPARα peaks that lack this heterotypic module
source: In addition, fasting-regulated genes with BCL6-PPARα regulatory elements exhibited significantly greater ranges of expression than those with PPARα peaks that lack this heterotypic module (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), and their ontology was particularly enriched for functions in lipid regulation and oxidative metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: Fasting-regulated genes with BCL6-PPARα regulatory elements are particularly enriched for functions in lipid regulation and oxidative metabolism
source: In addition, fasting-regulated genes with BCL6-PPARα regulatory elements exhibited significantly greater ranges of expression than those with PPARα peaks that lack this heterotypic module (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), and their ontology was particularly enriched for functions in lipid regulation and oxidative metabolism (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: PPARα is critical for the fasting induction of genes mediating peroxisomal and mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation as well as microsomal ω-hydroxylation
source: PPARα is critical for the fasting induction of genes mediating peroxisomal and mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation as well as microsomal ω-hydroxylation (Contreras et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2015; Hardwick et al., 2009; Hashimoto et al., 2000; Kersten et al., 1999; Leone et al., 1999; Montagner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Contreras et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2015; Hardwick et al., 2009; Hashimoto et al., 2000; Kersten et al., 1999; Leone et al., 1999; Montagner et al., 2016

claim: Loss of Bcl6 rescued 209 of 795 dysregulated genes in fasted Ppara-/- mice
source: RNA-seq revealed that loss of Bcl6 rescued 209 of 795 dysregulated genes in fasted Ppara-/- mice compared to fasted controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Bcl6 deletion restored expression of genes involved in monocarboxylic acid and lipoprotein metabolism; ketone body synthesis; AMPK and PPAR signaling; and peroxisomes in Ppara-/- mice
source: Among genes normally upregulated with fasting, Bcl6 deletion restored expression of genes involved in monocarboxylic acid and lipoprotein metabolism; ketone body synthesis; AMPK and PPAR signaling; and peroxisomes (Figure 5B, top panel).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Loss of Bcl6 restores expression at a subset of PPARα-directed genes controlling lipid metabolism in Ppara-/- mice
source: Thus, loss of Bcl6 restores expression at a subset of PPARα-directed genes controlling lipid metabolism.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice

claim: H3K27ac is reestablished or enhanced at BCL6-PPARα-binding sites in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO livers
source: Fasting-induced genes with impaired expression in Ppara-/- mice demonstrated low H3K27ac signal around BCL6-PPARα-binding sites in Ppara-/- compared to control mice. By contrast, in livers of Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO animals, H3K27ac is reestablished or even enhanced at these sites (Figure 5C, top left panel; and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A

claim: BCL6 de-repression restores aberrant liver cis-regulatory activity in Ppara-/- mice along fasting responsive genes
source: Thus, BCL6 de-repression restores aberrant liver cis-regulatory activity in Ppara-/- mice along fasting responsive genes.
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq data in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice

claim: HDAC3 was substantially diminished at BCL6-PPARα sites along rescued fasting genes in the absence of Bcl6
source: Since hepatocyte BCL6 binds to SMRT/NCoR-HDAC3 at a subset of its binding sites (Figure 3C and D), we specifically examined HDAC3 occupancy at BCL6-PPARα peaks along rescued fasting genes. In the absence of Bcl6, HDAC3 was substantially diminished at these BCL6-PPARα sites (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by HDAC3 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Ppard levels were significantly increased in fasted Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO compared to Ppara-/- mice
source: Using qPCR, we found that Ppard levels were significantly increased in fasted Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO compared to Ppara-/- mice, while Pparg levels were unchanged (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Pparg levels were unchanged in fasted Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO compared to Ppara-/- mice
source: Using qPCR, we found that Ppard levels were significantly increased in fasted Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO compared to Ppara-/- mice, while Pparg levels were unchanged (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E

claim: BCL6 binds multiple intronic sites along the Ppard gene
source: Moreover, BCL6 ChIP-sequencing revealed that BCL6 binds multiple intronic sites along the Ppard gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that it directly represses Ppard expression.
evidence: Supported by BCL6 ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: BCL6 directly represses Ppard expression
source: Moreover, BCL6 ChIP-sequencing revealed that BCL6 binds multiple intronic sites along the Ppard gene (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that it directly represses Ppard expression.
evidence: Supported by BCL6 ChIP-seq data and qPCR showing increased Ppard expression in Bcl6LKO mice

claim: PPARδ binding was increased near rescued genes in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO compared to Ppara-/- mice
source: Consistent with their enhanced Ppard levels, we observed increased PPARδ binding near rescued genes in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO compared to Ppara-/- mice (Figure 5C, right panel), particularly at upregulated fasting genes (Figure 5F), including Acot2, (Figure 5G), Hmgcs2, Aldh3a2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), and others (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by PPARδ ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C, 5F, 5G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and E

claim: Loss of BCL6 directly relieves repression and potentiates PPARδ-mediated transactivation to restore fasting liver gene expression in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice
source: Together, these observations identified that loss of BCL6 directly relieves repression and potentiates PPARδ-mediated transactivation to restore fasting liver gene expression in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice.
evidence: Supported by multiple ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing loss of HDAC3, increased PPARδ binding, and restored gene expression

claim: Ad libitum fed Bcl6LKO mice exhibited higher circulating ketone bodies compared to Bcl6fl/fl mice
source: Ad libitum fed Bcl6LKO mice exhibited higher circulating ketone bodies compared to Bcl6fl/fl mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ketone body measurements shown in Figure 6A

claim: Mice lacking hepatic Bcl6 have higher rates of complete fatty acid oxidation
source: Additionally, mice lacking hepatic Bcl6 have higher rates of complete fatty acid oxidation as measured by oxidation of 14C-palmitate in liver homogenates (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by fatty acid oxidation assays shown in Figure 6B

claim: Bcl6LKO mice showed no differences in fatty acid uptake, triglyceride secretion, and hepatic lipogenesis compared to controls
source: In contrast, analysis of fatty acid uptake, triglyceride secretion, and hepatic lipogenesis based on in vivo deuterium incorporation revealed no other differences in lipid metabolism between Bcl6LKO mice and controls (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by lipid uptake, secretion, and lipogenesis assays shown in Figure 6C-E

claim: Bcl6LKO mice were profoundly protected from developing steatosis after 19 weeks of high-fat diet
source: Bcl6LKO mice were profoundly protected from developing steatosis, as demonstrated by oil red O staining and more than a 50% reduction in hepatic triglyceride content compared to Bcl6fl/fl controls, despite similar increases in body weight (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 6F-H

claim: Bcl6LKO mice showed more than a 50% reduction in hepatic triglyceride content compared to controls after high-fat diet
source: Bcl6LKO mice were profoundly protected from developing steatosis, as demonstrated by oil red O staining and more than a 50% reduction in hepatic triglyceride content compared to Bcl6fl/fl controls, despite similar increases in body weight (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 6G

claim: HFD-exposed Bcl6LKO mice exhibited significantly lower levels of fasting serum glucose
source: Accompanying these reductions in hepatic lipid accumulation, HFD-exposed Bcl6LKO mice exhibited significantly lower levels of fasting serum glucose (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and a non-significant reduction in insulin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by glucose measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: Bcl6LKO mice exhibited a trend towards enhanced insulin responsiveness when challenged with 5-week HFD
source: Moreover, when challenged with a shorter term 5-week HFD, Bcl6LKO mice exhibited a trend towards enhanced insulin responsiveness, as measured by levels of phosphorylated AKT following acute administration of exogenous insulin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of phosphorylated AKT shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Mice lacking hepatic Bcl6 have heightened capacity to catabolize lipids via β-oxidation and subsequent ketogenesis or TCA cycling
source: These combined observations demonstrate that mice lacking hepatic Bcl6 have heightened capacity to catabolize lipids via β-oxidation and subsequent ketogenesis or TCA cycling, as well as improved glucose homeostasis when challenged with high-fat diet.
evidence: Supported by multiple functional assays including fatty acid oxidation and ketone body measurements

claim: Mice lacking hepatic Bcl6 have improved glucose homeostasis when challenged with high-fat diet
source: These combined observations demonstrate that mice lacking hepatic Bcl6 have heightened capacity to catabolize lipids via β-oxidation and subsequent ketogenesis or TCA cycling, as well as improved glucose homeostasis when challenged with high-fat diet.
evidence: Supported by glucose and insulin measurements in high-fat diet fed mice

claim: Ppara-/- mice exhibit fasting hypoketonemia and impaired fatty acid oxidation leading to steatosis
source: Ppara-/- mice exhibit fasting hypoketonemia and impaired fatty acid oxidation leading to steatosis (Gao et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2000; Kersten et al., 1999; Leone et al., 1999; Montagner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gao et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2000; Kersten et al., 1999; Leone et al., 1999; Montagner et al., 2016

claim: After 48 hr of fasting, Ppara-/- mice developed centrilobular macrosteatosis
source: After 48 hr of fasting, Ppara-/- mice developed centrilobular macrosteatosis (Figure 6I), as previously reported (Hashimoto et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6I and citation to Hashimoto et al., 2000

claim: Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO animals were strongly protected from hepatic triglyceride accumulation after 48 hr fasting
source: Remarkably, Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO animals were strongly protected from hepatic triglyceride accumulation based upon histological analysis with oil red O staining and demonstrated 23% reduced triglyceride accumulation compared to Ppara-/- mice (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 6I and J

claim: Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO animals demonstrated 23% reduced triglyceride accumulation compared to Ppara-/- mice after 48 hr fasting
source: Remarkably, Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO animals were strongly protected from hepatic triglyceride accumulation based upon histological analysis with oil red O staining and demonstrated 23% reduced triglyceride accumulation compared to Ppara-/- mice (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: Supported by triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 6J

claim: Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice had higher rates of 14C-palmitate oxidation in liver homogenates compared to fasted Ppara-/- mice
source: Compared to fasted Ppara-/- mice, Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice also had higher rates of 14C-palmitate oxidation in liver homogenates, exhibited in both completely oxidized 14CO2 and incompletely oxidized 14C-acid soluble intermediates (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by fatty acid oxidation assays shown in Figure 6K

claim: Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice revealed higher ketone body levels compared to Ppara-/- mice
source: In line with their reduced lipid accrual, Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice also revealed higher ketone body levels (Figure 6L), suggesting that ablation of Bcl6 can de-repress ketone body synthesis even in the absence of Ppara.
evidence: Supported by ketone body measurements shown in Figure 6L

claim: Ablation of Bcl6 can de-repress ketone body synthesis even in the absence of Ppara
source: In line with their reduced lipid accrual, Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice also revealed higher ketone body levels (Figure 6L), suggesting that ablation of Bcl6 can de-repress ketone body synthesis even in the absence of Ppara.
evidence: Supported by ketone body measurements in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice shown in Figure 6L

claim: Loss of liver Bcl6 rescues metabolic defects of Ppara deficiency
source: Overall, these results established that loss of liver Bcl6 rescues metabolic defects of Ppara deficiency.
evidence: Supported by multiple functional assays in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice

claim: BCL6 converges with PPARα at over 13,000 regulatory regions
source: On a genome-wide scale, BCL6 converges with PPARα at over 13,000 regulatory regions on which BCL6 binding is enriched with feeding, whereas PPARα is induced by fasting.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing overlapping binding sites

claim: The BCL6-PPARα cis-regulatory module annotates to over 1,400 fasting-responsive genes
source: This dynamic BCL6-PPARα cis-regulatory module annotates to over 1,400 fasting-responsive genes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Bcl6 ablation mimics the fasting transcriptional response
source: Moreover, Bcl6 ablation mimics the fasting transcriptional response, and a myriad of defects in Ppara-/- mice are partially rescued by concomitant deletion of hepatocyte Bcl6, ranging from defective fasting enhancer activity and gene expression to impaired fatty acid oxidation, hypoketonemia, and susceptibility to steatosis.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparing Bcl6LKO and fasted mice

claim: BCL6 functions outside of hematopoietic cells were poorly defined prior to this study
source: Previously, BCL6 functions outside of hematopoietic cells were poorly defined.
evidence: Supported by literature review

claim: BCL6 competes with STAT5 and modulates responses to growth hormone and drug metabolism in liver
source: In liver, prior analysis supported a role for BCL6 in competing with STAT5 and modulating responses to growth hormone and drug metabolism (Chikada et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chikada et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012

claim: Over 80% of Bcl6-/- mice exhibit myocarditis
source: Over 80% of Bcl6-/- mice exhibit myocarditis and over 70% have pulmonary vasculitis with elevated levels of IL-4,–5, and −13, cytokines known to directly impact liver metabolism (Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2010; Stanya et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to characterization of Bcl6-/- mice and citations to Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2010; Stanya et al., 2013

claim: Over 70% of Bcl6-/- mice have pulmonary vasculitis with elevated levels of IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13
source: Over 80% of Bcl6-/- mice exhibit myocarditis and over 70% have pulmonary vasculitis with elevated levels of IL-4,–5, and −13, cytokines known to directly impact liver metabolism (Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2010; Stanya et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to characterization of Bcl6-/- mice and citations to Ricardo-Gonzalez et al., 2010; Stanya et al., 2013

claim: Loss of Bcl6 in hepatocytes causes cell-autonomous enhancement of fatty acid oxidation without a direct impact on lipid synthesis
source: Using genetic, genomic, and isotopic analyses we reveal that loss of Bcl6 in hepatocytes causes cell-autonomous enhancement of fatty acid oxidation without a direct impact on lipid synthesis.
evidence: Supported by fatty acid oxidation assays and lipogenesis measurements in Bcl6LKO mice

claim: Physical interactions between BCL6 and various cofactors have been well documented in immune cells
source: Physical interactions between BCL6 and various cofactors have been well documented and in immune cells mediate distinct functional roles (Huang et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huang et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2013

claim: SMRT and NCoR bind to the BCL6 N-terminal BTB domain
source: Among these interaction partners are SMRT and NCoR, which bind to the BCL6 N-terminal BTB domain and function as scaffolds to recruit HDAC3 and other corepressive machinery (Perissi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perissi et al., 2010

claim: SMRT and NCoR function as scaffolds to recruit HDAC3 and other corepressive machinery
source: Among these interaction partners are SMRT and NCoR, which bind to the BCL6 N-terminal BTB domain and function as scaffolds to recruit HDAC3 and other corepressive machinery (Perissi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perissi et al., 2010

claim: Nearly 80% overlap exists between BCL6 and the cistromes of SMRT, NCoR, and HDAC3 in liver
source: In liver, we found nearly 80% overlap between BCL6 and the cistromes of SMRT, NCoR, and HDAC3.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis

claim: Thousands of SMRT, HDAC3, and particularly NCoR binding peaks were independent of BCL6
source: However, thousands of SMRT, HDAC3, and particularly NCoR binding peaks were independent of BCL6.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis

claim: SMRT, NCoR, and HDAC3 may frequently engage multiple transcription factor complexes within a single regulatory region
source: Furthermore, even at regulatory regions where BCL6 and these coregulators colocalize, persistent ChIP-seq signals for SMRT, NCoR, and HDAC3 are often observed in the genetic absence of Bcl6. These findings indicate that SMRT, NCoR, and HDAC3 may frequently engage multiple transcription factor complexes within a single regulatory region.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data in Bcl6LKO mice showing persistent corepressor binding

claim: Knockouts and various knockin mutants of NCoR, SMRT, and HDAC3 have demonstrated hepatic steatosis phenotypes
source: Indeed, knockouts and various knockin mutants of NCoR, SMRT, and HDAC3 have demonstrated hepatic steatosis phenotypes (Knutson et al., 2008; Mottis et al., 2013; Shimizu et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2012), in contrast to the lipid overload-protected phenotype observed here with hepatocyte Bcl6 ablation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Knutson et al., 2008; Mottis et al., 2013; Shimizu et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2012

claim: The clustering of transcription factors at regulatory regions has been proposed as a flexible mechanism to control diverse gene expression patterns
source: The clustering of transcription factors at regulatory regions has been proposed as a flexible mechanism to control diverse gene expression patterns during development and in response to environmental stimulus (Arnone and Davidson, 1997; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arnone and Davidson, 1997; Smith et al., 2013

claim: PPARδ was reported to physically interact with BCL6
source: PPARα is the predominant PPAR isotype in liver, while PPARδ is expressed at lower levels but was reported to physically interact with BCL6 (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2003

claim: Ppara and Ppard are each genetically dispensable for chromatin recruitment of BCL6
source: However, we find that Ppara and Ppard are each genetically dispensable for chromatin recruitment of BCL6.
evidence: Supported by BCL6 ChIP-seq data in Ppara-/- and PpardLKO mice

claim: BCL6 opposition to PPARα occurs via proximate binding at independent cis-regulatory elements
source: Thus, BCL6 opposition to PPARα occurs via proximate binding at independent cis-regulatory elements, a mechanism distinct from FXR, which has been reported to counter PPARα transcriptional outputs through competition for DR1-binding sites (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing independent binding and citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: FXR counters PPARα transcriptional outputs through competition for DR1-binding sites
source: Thus, BCL6 opposition to PPARα occurs via proximate binding at independent cis-regulatory elements, a mechanism distinct from FXR, which has been reported to counter PPARα transcriptional outputs through competition for DR1-binding sites (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2014

claim: The regulatory interaction between BCL6 and PPARα is unique from HNF6 and REV-ERBα, which cooperatively repress transcription via tethering
source: The regulatory interaction between BCL6 and PPARα is also unique from other integrative regulators of hepatic lipid metabolism such as HNF6 and REV-ERBα, which cooperatively repress transcription via tethering (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016 and comparison to BCL6-PPARα mechanism

claim: BCL6-PPAR elements in fasting enhancers endow them with variably repressive or activating regulatory potential
source: We speculate that BCL6-PPAR elements in fasting enhancers endow them with variably repressive or activating regulatory potential, contributing to highly dynamic gene expression across the feeding to fasting transition.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing dynamic binding and gene expression patterns

claim: Genetic ablation of Bcl6 de-represses BCL6-PPAR regulatory regions and compensates for loss of PPARα transactivity in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice
source: In a related manner, genetic ablation of Bcl6 de-represses these regulatory regions and compensates for loss of PPARα transactivity in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice.
evidence: Supported by H3K27ac ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data in Ppara-/-;Bcl6LKO mice

claim: Liver metabolic shifts are not simply directed by inducible transactivating factors
source: Thus, we find that liver metabolic shifts are not simply directed by inducible transactivating factors.
evidence: Supported by the discovery of BCL6 as a key repressor in metabolic regulation

claim: 'Active repression' by BCL6 and its dynamic modulation play key roles in toggling between the fed and fasted state
source: Rather, 'active repression' (Hanna-Rose and Hansen, 1996) by BCL6 and its dynamic modulation play key additional roles in toggling between the fed and fasted state and determining hepatic lipid accumulation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq and functional data showing BCL6's role in metabolic regulation and citation to Hanna-Rose and Hansen, 1996

claim: Inhibitors of BCL6 have been developed to target BCL6 and selective interactions with its corepressors
source: Since inhibitors of BCL6 have been developed to target BCL6 and selective interactions with its corepressors (Cardenas et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2018), these findings also raise the possibility that BCL6 de-repression could represent a future therapeutic strategy for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence: Supported by citations to Cardenas et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2018

claim: BCL6 de-repression could represent a future therapeutic strategy for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
source: Since inhibitors of BCL6 have been developed to target BCL6 and selective interactions with its corepressors (Cardenas et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2018), these findings also raise the possibility that BCL6 de-repression could represent a future therapeutic strategy for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence: Supported by functional data showing protection from steatosis in Bcl6LKO mice
